newsitem.title: CHINA: China party chief vows economic, political reforms.
newsitem.headline: China party chief vows economic, political reforms.

text.p: China's Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin on Thursday pledged more economic and political reforms, setting the tone for a crucial party congress later this year.
"There must be new breakthroughs in reform of the economic system," Jiang told the Central Party School, the main training ground for senior party officials.
"(We) must continue to push forward reform of the political system," the Xinhua news agency quoted Jiang as saying. He did not elaborate.
Chinese sources said the Communist Party would unveil a bold plan to reduce the role of the state sector in the economy at its 15th congress in the second half of this year.

China has gradually reduced the role of the state sector in the economy and boosted that of private and collective enterprises since it abandoned Soviet-style central planning and embraced market reforms almost two decades ago.
"We must open up and keep forging ahead and must not stick to old ways," Jiang said.
One Chinese analyst said Jiang's speech to the Central Party School would set the tone for the 15th party congress, where key policies and personnel changes for the next five years will be made.
Jiang, the handpicked successor of late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, held high Deng's banner of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
"Whatever difficulties or risk we meet, we will not waver ... from Deng Xiaoping's socialism with Chinese characteristics," Jiang said.
Socialism with Chinese characteristics is the fig-leaf phrase Deng coined to justify such un-Marxist concepts as free markets, private enterprise and stock exchanges.
Jiang said Marxism was not infallible but China still needed it.
"Marxism ... is not unalterable, he said. "(But) Marxism and Mao Zedong thought must not be thrown away. (We) will lose our roots and walk the path of evil if we dump them."
Jiang vowed to intensify the war against corruption.
"The fight against corruption is a serious political struggle that relates to the life and death of the party and the state," Jiang said.
"(We) must further intensify it and resolutely and unremittingly continue with it."
Corruption, virtually eliminated in the years after the communists came to power in 1949, has staged a comeback in recent years in the wake of economic reforms.
Jiang called for solidarity in the face of difficulties.

Diplomats have said his planned policy and personnel changes at the coming congress would encounter strong resistance -- from rivals who will oppose him for the sake of power or from leftists opposed on principle.

Jiang, who is also the state president and chairman of the party's Central Military Commission, must use the congress to set his own stamp on party politics and win his stripes as well as endorsement for his position as Deng's heir, analysts said.
The congress will set the path of the world's most populous nation as it begins a new era without Deng or other veterans of the revolutionary generation of Mao Zedong.
Deng died in February aged 92.
